# **CHAPTER I**

# **INTRODUCTION**

### **1.0 Project Purpose** 

SmartFlow is being proposed to help with the ongoing lack of real time awareness and accountability when physical transfer of financial and administrative papers happens among the Engineering , Human Resources (HR), Budget, and Accounting offices of the Municipality of Urbiztondo. Right now, the way documents get routed still leans on manual follow ups , like calls messages and sometimes in person checking, which in turn causes processing lags , wasted time, unclear who is responsible during each handoff, and a late consolidation process that we need for COA related monitoring and also for report preparation.

The purpose of this project is to develop a QR-based inter-department document flow tracking and COA compliance support system. The system shall log every handoff with exact timestamps and named personnel, show processing status through monitoring dashboards, and produce COA-aligned document flow summaries. Day-to-day operations including registration, QR scanning, per-office monitoring, alerts, and reports shall be performed through an Android mobile application used by frontline staff and department heads. Administrative monitoring for the Municipal Accountant (who also serves as the LGU system administrator for SmartFlow) shall be provided through a web-based administrative dashboard  on the municipal local area network (LAN), sharing the same PHP/MySQL backend. The Prototype implements the mobile client and server API; the dedicated web administrative dashboard is part of the proposed system design and is deferred to a future development phase, during which administrators may use the mobile application for monitoring in the pilot. In the end, SmartFlow is meant to raise efficiency, transparency, and accountability in document handling. 

### **1.1 Project Description** 

The municipality of Urbiztondo has designed this kind of QR-based inter department document flow tracing , and compliance system, to make things more visible, smoother, and more accountable for the financial and administrative document movement across the engineering office, the human resources (HR) team, budget, and accounting units.  

Currently, most documents (including disbursement records, payroll records, and approved budgets) are carried physically from one office to the next, with no real-time tracking, and this is what can create delays , a weaker accountability, and a kind of heavy dependence on manual chasing later, by phone calls, quick messages, or just showing up in person.  

SmartFlow is intended to ease those issues by giving each document a single QR code at the point of origin. Each QR label encodes a cryptographically signed token — not a plain document ID — so that tampered or forged labels are rejected by the server. Tokens carry an expiration period, and expired labels are refused with a clear error message. Every time the document is handed to another department, the receiving side will scan it using a phone, and then it will log a set of details like the document identity tied to the origin office, the staff members who handled the document, and the exact time stamp of when it was scanned into that office. The system enforces state-based scan rules so that only a valid transition is accepted per scan — for example, a document already marked IN cannot be scanned IN again — and all rejected scans, including duplicate attempts, expired labels, and tampered codes, are logged with reason codes for audit review. In effect, this will form a real-time audit track of where the document has been, and when.

SmartFlow follows a dual-client design. Frontline personnel and department heads use the mobile application at the counter and during handoffs to register documents, scan QR codes, and view office-level dashboards, alerts, and reports. The Municipal Accountant, who also serves as the LGU system administrator, is intended to use a web-based administrative dashboard in a desktop browser on the LAN for municipal-wide visibility, consolidation, and COA-oriented summaries. Both clients connect to the same centralized PHP/MySQL server. Printable QR labels may be generated through a desktop browser without replacing mobile scanning as the primary workflow. 

### **1.2 Objective of the Study** 

This study aims to develop and evaluate SmartFlow as a tracking and COA compliance support solution to improve the efficiency, transparency, and accountability of inter departmental document movement in the Municipality of Urbiztondo. 

### **1.2.1 General Objective of the Study** 

The general objective of this study is to develop and implement a QR-based inter-departmental document flow-tracking system with COA-compliance support features that improve transparency, efficiency, and accountability in the handling of financial and administrative documents in the Municipality of Urbiztondo.

### **1.2.2 Specific Objectives of the Study**

Specifically, this study aims to:

* Generate a cryptographically signed QR token for every document when it is created, with a built-in expiration period and server-side signature verification to prevent tampering and forgery.  
* Create a scan-and-track feature that records document transfers, including document identity, office, personnel, and time received, and enforces state-based scan rules so that only valid IN/OUT transitions are accepted per document state.  
* Prevent duplicate scans through a state matrix and debounce logic, and log all rejected scan attempts — including duplicates, expired tokens, and tampered labels — with reason codes.  
* Develop an Android dashboard to show document status, current location, and processing time for staff and department heads.  
* Design a web-based admin dashboard for the Municipal Accountant (acting as system administrator) for overall monitoring and COA reporting.  
* Add an alert system for documents that take too long to process.  
* Generate reports showing document counts, processing times, completion rates, and delays based on COA requirements.  
* Provide analytics to measure office performance and identify processing bottlenecks.  
* Evaluate the system's usability and effectiveness through feedback from frontline staff, department heads, and the Municipal Accountant (system administrator).

### **1.3 Significance of the Study** 

This study is significant because it addresses a common operational issue in Local Government Units (LGUs): documents move physically across offices, yet performance, accountability, and compliance are difficult to monitor without an organized tracking mechanism. Through the development of a QR-based document flow tracking system with scan-based audit trails and monitoring summaries aligned with Commission on Audit (COA) preparation requirements, SmartFlow supports faster coordination, minimizes reliance on manual follow-ups, and strengthens transparency in document handling. Furthermore, the system helps reduce the risk of Audit Observation Reports (AORs) caused by delayed, missing, or improperly tracked supporting documents during auditing and compliance preparation.

The study will benefit the following:

***A. For the Municipality of Urbiztondo and Municipal Management***

The study provides the municipality with a more efficient and transparent method of monitoring document movement across departments. Through centralized tracking, municipal management can identify processing delays, improve inter-office coordination, strengthen internal controls, and support better decision-making through generated analytics and monitoring summaries.

***B. For the Municipal Accountant and Accounting Staff***

The system reduces the time spent conducting manual follow-ups and verifying document locations. It improves visibility of incoming and outgoing requirements and supports faster consolidation of records through automated summaries and a web-based administrative dashboard. This contributes to more organized financial document handling and improved compliance preparation.

***C. For Department Heads (Engineering, Human Resource, and Budget Offices)***

The system enables department heads to monitor office-level processing times, pending transactions, and overdue documents using the mobile application. This supports workload management, accountability, and compliance with internal office procedures and audit-related requirements.

D. ***For Frontline Staff and Employees***

The study benefits frontline personnel by providing proof of document forwarding and clearer accountability during document handoffs through QR-based scanning. It minimizes repeated status inquiries, reduces confusion in document routing, and simplifies daily document-processing tasks.

***E. For the Municipal Accountant as System Administrator*** 

The system assists the Municipal Accountant, in her additional role as system administrator, in managing user account provisioning, role and office assignments, and processing-time thresholds, as well as in coordinating with LGU IT on server deployment and database maintenance. It also provides a structured framework for maintaining secure and organized digital records within the municipality.

***F. For the Commission on Audit (COA)***

The Commission on Audit benefits indirectly through improved timeliness, traceability, and consistency in document flow management. By maintaining organized audit trails and monitoring records, the system helps the LGU minimize Audit Observation Reports (AORs) related to delayed, missing, or improperly tracked supporting documents during audit preparation and compliance checking.

 G. For the Students and Faculty of National Teachers College

This study contributes to the academic and technological advancement of students and faculty members of National Teachers College by providing a practical example of how information technology solutions can address real-world government operational challenges. The project serves as a learning reference for students in developing systems related to workflow automation, QR technology, mobile applications, and web-based monitoring platforms. Faculty members may also use the study as supporting material for future discussions, research, and innovation in information systems and e-governance technologies.

 H. For Future Researchers and Developers

The study provides future researchers and developers with a reference model for designing practical and low-disruption workflow-tracking systems for LGUs and similar organizations. It contributes knowledge on integrating QR-based tracking, mobile field operations, and web-based administrative oversight to improve transparency, accountability, and operational efficiency in document management processes.

### **1.4.1 Scope of the Study**

### The study focuses on the development of SmartFlow, a QR-based inter-department document flow tracking and COA compliance support system for the Municipality of Urbiztondo. The system is designed to improve the monitoring, tracking, and accountability of financial and administrative documents transferred among municipal offices.

### Specifically, the study covers the following:

* ### The development of a QR code-based document tracking system for monitoring document movement between departments, using cryptographically signed QR tokens with expiration to prevent tampering and unauthorized reuse.

* ### The implementation of a Flutter mobile application for scanning QR codes and recording document receive and forward transactions, with server-side token verification and state-based scan validation at every handoff.

* ### The development of a web-based administrative dashboard for document registration, monitoring, alerts, and report generation.

* ### The use of PHP, MySQL, and Apache Server as the backend technologies for data storage and system processing.

* ### The monitoring of document processing time, delayed documents, completion rates, and document movement history.

* ### The generation of COA-oriented document flow summaries and reports for monitoring and compliance support.

* ### The recording of audit trail information including office, personnel, timestamp, document status, and scan result (accepted or rejected with reason code) during every handoff, accessible through a QR scan monitor dashboard for administrative review.

* ### The evaluation of the system using ISO/IEC 25010 software quality standards through user acceptance testing.

### 

### 

### **1.4.2 Limitation** 

The study is limited to the following:

* The system only covers financial and administrative documents related to COA monitoring and reporting.  
* The study is limited to the following offices:  
- Accounting Department  
- Budget Department  
- Human Resource (HR) Department  
- Engineering Department  
* The system only uses QR code scanning. Advanced technologies such as RFID and NFC are not included in the study.  
* The system only generates document monitoring summaries such as processing time, delayed documents, and completion rates. It does not generate official financial statements.  
* Hardware procurement, internet hosting, and full system deployment are outside the scope of the study and will depend on the LGU.   
* The accuracy of the system depends on proper and consistent scanning during every document handoff. Missed scans may result in incomplete tracking data.  
* The study only focuses on document tracking and monitoring. It does not replace existing approval, signature, or official document processing procedures.

 

### **1.5 Review of Related Literature** 

**Local Studies**

Several local studies highlight how digital technologies help, in a more practical way, improving the efficiency of handling documents, and also monitoring activities inside government institutions. 

## **Acedo, G. G., et al. (2025).** Acedo et al. developed a web-based document tracking system with QR-code technology for Catanduanes State University. Each document received a unique QR code so staff could monitor status in real time instead of searching physical files. The researchers evaluated the system using ISO/IEC 25010 and reported an excellent overall rating. This study supports SmartFlow’s use of QR tagging, a centralized database, and ISO-based pilot evaluation. SmartFlow differs because it targets municipal financial documents among Engineering, HR, Budget, and Accounting in Urbiztondo, with Flutter used for scanning at handoffs and React for registration, dashboards, and COA-oriented reports. 

## **Piloton, A. J. L., et al. (2023).** Piloton et al. built a records tracking management system with QR code technology to replace manual logbooks in a government records environment. The system tracked file movement, verified users, and maintained an audit trail of who handled each record. Evaluators gave positive feedback on usability and accountability. SmartFlow adopts the same principle at every inter-department handoff for disbursement vouchers, payroll records, and approved budgets. Scan events are sent to a PHP REST API and stored in MySQL for reporting on the web portal.

## **Aisporna, M. R., & Malicdem, E. K. (2024).** Aisporna and Malicdem implemented a web-based document routing and tracking system (DRTS) with a workflow management algorithm for the Local Government Unit of Magallanes, Philippines. The system improved processing speed and accountability between departments and was rated highly acceptable by users. Among local studies, this is the strongest precedent for SmartFlow because it addresses LGU inter-department routing, not only a school or single office. SmartFlow extends the model with Flutter scan-in and scan-out on physical folders and COA-aligned flow summary reports for the Municipal Accountant.

## **Urmeneta, J. A., Agullo, J., et al. (2025).** Urmeneta et al. designed a digitized document tracking system that integrates QR code technology to record each movement in a verifiable audit trail. The study concluded that automated logging improves transparency and makes it easier to validate document history during review. SmartFlow applies the same accountability goal for Urbiztondo. The system does not digitize or store the content of voucher or payroll pages; it tracks only the movement of the paper packet, which matches the municipality’s current workflow.

## **Castro, R. B., et al. (2022).** Castro et al. created a web-based document tracking system using barcode technology with SMS notification when document status changed. The system identified which unit currently held a document and reduced uncertainty during routing between locations. SmartFlow uses QR codes on a Flutter mobile application and web-based alerts on the React portal instead of SMS, which avoids extra telecom cost and fits staff who already use smartphones. The study still confirms that automated notifications reduce the burden of manual follow-up.

## **Balangat, E. S. (2022).** Balangat evaluated the records management system of LGU Calanasan and reported delayed submissions, poor accessibility of records, and lack of transparency in routing. These findings closely match the interview with the Municipal Accountant of Urbiztondo, who cited late documents from other departments and consolidation delays using Excel. SmartFlow addresses this gap through real-time location on the dashboard, overdue flags, and department performance analytics that show which office repeatedly slows the flow.

## **Tabia, V. U. (2022).** Tabia examined records management and data security in local government units and emphasized proper custody, accountability, and protection of government information. The study supports designing systems that log custody events without exposing unnecessary personal data. SmartFlow logs office name, personnel, timestamp, and document identifier on each scan, while QR labels show only a tracking ID. Access to dashboards and exports is limited by role on the web application.

## **Web-based document tracking system,** DPWH Laguna II District Engineering Office (Philippine EJournals, 2022). Researchers developed a web-based system to register, track, and retrieve documents within a government engineering office. The study demonstrated that centralized tracking improves retrieval, reduces lost files, and strengthens control over document status. SmartFlow applies the same principle across four municipal offices and three financial document types that support COA preparation, rather than a single district engineering unit alone.

## **Docu-Go:** Web-based barangay document requesting system (IJITC, 2024). Docu-Go is a web-based system that allows residents to submit document requests and check status online, which reduces repeated visits and phone inquiries at the barangay hall. Although the context is barangay frontline service, the lesson applies inside Urbiztondo: staff currently use calls and group chats to ask whether a voucher or payroll packet was received. SmartFlow replaces informal status checks with logged scans and a shared React dashboard visible to authorized offices.

## **Gedorio, B. S., et al. (2023).** Gedorio et al. evaluated a local government–related software system using the ISO/IEC 25010 software quality model and reported strong ratings in usability, reliability, and other characteristics. The results support using the same evaluation framework for LGU pilot systems. SmartFlow will use ISO/IEC 25010 during pilot testing with Accounting staff, department heads, and frontline clerks who perform daily scanning on Flutter.

**Foreign Studies**

## **Abdrabou-Adnan, L. (2023).** In Digitalization and Usage of QR-Code System in Documents Management, Abdrabou-Adnan linked each physical document file to a QR code so workers no longer searched through large paper stacks to find custody information. The study supports a hybrid model in which paper remains the legal record but digital logs show location and history. SmartFlow uses the same approach for disbursement vouchers, payroll records, and approved budgets moving among municipal departments in Urbiztondo.

## **Peltokorpi, J., e. atl  (2021).** Peltokorpi et al., in QR Code-Based Material Flow Monitoring in a Subcontractor Manufacturer Network, showed that QR scanning at multiple sites can feed a central database for monitoring material flow across a network. In an LGU, each department office acts like a node in a routing network. SmartFlow treats Engineering, HR, Budget, and Accounting as nodes, with Flutter scans at each handoff and one PHP/MySQL server for centralized monitoring on React.

## **Hernandez, C., et al. (2023).** Hernandez et al. implemented QR codes with a centralized monitoring dashboard to improve tracking accuracy and data accessibility for decision-makers. Field staff captured events through mobile scanning while administrators viewed summaries online. SmartFlow follows the same architecture: decentralized scanning at each office and centralized monitoring for the Municipal Accountant, who also serves as the system administrator, on the web portal. 

## **Li, X., et al. (2024).** Li et al. discussed security risks in QR-based document systems, including tampering, spoofing, and technical protections such as watermarking. Payroll and disbursement packets are sensitive even when only movement is tracked. SmartFlow addresses these risks through HMAC-SHA256 signed tokens (`SF1.{payload}.{hmac}`) that are verified server-side on every scan; tampered or forged labels are rejected before any record is written. Tokens expire after a fixed period, and expired labels are refused with a clear error message. While watermarking is not implemented, the signed-token approach directly counters the tampering and spoofing risks identified in this literature.

## **Lobonț, O., et al. (2025).** Lobonț et al. reported that office monitoring and compliance systems fail when employees skip required steps in the procedure. Document tracking depends on consistent behavior at every receive and forward event. SmartFlow therefore requires a scan at every handoff and includes training for users with low technology knowledge, as noted by the Municipal Accountant during needs assessment.

## **Marian, et al. (2025).** Marian et al. described audit flows that record which user accessed or moved a document and at what time, creating a defensible chain of custody. SmartFlow produces a similar trail through scan-in and scan-out logs with document identifier, office, personnel, and timestamp for Engineering, HR, Budget, and Accounting.

## **Alsuhibany, S. (2025).** Alsuhibany cautioned that QR-based solutions alone cannot verify every legal or financial aspect of the content inside a high-stakes document. SmartFlow is scoped correctly as a movement and compliance support tool: it proves where and when a physical document traveled to support COA preparation, not the numerical correctness of financial statements, which remain the responsibility of the Accounting office.

## **United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs (2024).** UN DESA e-government materials recommend measuring turnaround time, overdue workload, and completion rates as part of digital government maturity. SmartFlow’s COA-aligned summary module reports these indicators per department, helping the Municipal Accountant and management see delays before audit deadlines.

## **International Organization for Standardization (2011)** ISO/IEC 25010\. As literature and as an evaluation framework, ISO/IEC 25010 defines eight software quality characteristics used worldwide. Local studies by Acedo et al. (2025) and Gedorio et al. (2023) applied this model successfully. SmartFlow pilot testing will use the same eight criteria to assess whether the hybrid system is fit for daily use in a small LGU.

## **Rimando, M. K. V., & Corpuz, R. R. (2022).** Rimando and Corpuz developed a real-time QR tracking system with added security features for documents in transit, including protections relevant to sensitive records. SmartFlow does not require watermarking in the first version, but the study supports protecting audit log integrity and access control for vouchers and payroll documents in a government setting.

### **1.6 Review of Related Studies** 

**Local Studies** 

**Acedo, G. G., et al. (2025).** Web-based document tracking system for Catanduanes State University with QR-code technology. (Implemented Capstone Project).   
A web-based document tracking system for Catanduanes State University using QR-code technology by G. G. Acedo et al. (2025) was made to see how physical documents can be monitored and located. The team used QR codes as an extra layer for tracing so the web-based system can track where files are in a more or less real-time way. They mentioned that once the QR codes were used, tracking became easier and finding files was way more efficient than doing it manually, which is how they usually did it before automation. They also reported that the overall web-based system got an “Excellent” rating when they checked it using ISO/IEC 25010 software quality standards. This result shows the solution is actually usable and dependable in real situations. From their analysis, the researchers concluded that automating the monitoring process can cut down delays and help handle institutional workflows a lot smoother without the usual gaps. This paper connects to SmartFlow because it backs up the idea of using QR-code tagging as a reliable tracking tool, and it also supports using ISO/IEC 25010 as the framework for judging system performance instead of just guessing. 

**Aisporna, M. R., & Malicdem, E. K. (2024).** Web-Based Document Routing and Tracking System (DRTS) with Workflow Management Algorithm for Local Government Unit of Magallanes, Philippines. (Implemented LGU Project).   
Aisporna and Malicdem (2024) based their study on a web-based document routing and tracking system for the LGU of Magallanes, Philippines which uses a simple workflow management algorithm to automate processes and avoid operational bottlenecks. The system is rated as "High Acceptable" against software quality standards, significantly increasing processing efficiency and organizational accountability. This study is therefore essential empirical evidence for the SmartFlow project to establish that digital interdepartmental routing can be a practical solution for Philippine local government units. Thus, these results provide a strong basis for the effective deployment and testing of the proposed system in a pilot study within LGU Urbiztondo.

**Castro, R. B., et al. (2022).** Web-based document tracking system using barcode technology with SMS notification. (Implemented Local Study). 

Castro et al. (2022) presented a web-based document tracking system that employed QR barcode technology to automate the chronological movement of paperwork across multiple documents within an organization, and also set up SMS Notification. They have created a model to track person-to-person and can tell you who has your document, how it is being transferred from one location or individual to another etc. With both high functionality and reliability ratings, this study proves highly advantageous to the SmartFlow project. The specificity of personnel tracking supports our designs for voucher and payroll packet monitoring among the various departments of LGU Urbiztondo. Additionally, their suggestion of having individual office identifiers closely relates to our method of using routing paths for each department to improve workflows and prevent operational backlogs.

**Censoro, K. C. (2021).** Document management system using OCR, clustering, and QR coding algorithms. (Master’s Thesis).   
The SmartFlow project is grounded in K. C. Censoro's thesis Automating Document Management of 2021\. Her research shows that a combination of character recognition, clustering methods and QR coding substantially increases administrative efficiency. The system channels files into secure digital repositories, effectively removing the need for manual data entry altogether, thus easing clerical burdens and work-related fatigue. These results are even more relevant because they directly correlate with our goal to make the Accounting & Budget offices in local governments more efficient. These digital aides can significantly reduce unnecessary paper trails, relieve mental loads off municipal employees' minds and task them with addressing more high-value work right within their departments.

**Cuarez, R., et al. (2025).** Web-based item tracking system using OCR and Levenshtein matching for verification.

Cuarez et al. (2025) developed a web-based tracking system that utilizes Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and Levenshtein distance algorithm to verify and match document information. The study highlighted the importance of integrating validation algorithms in tracking systems to ensure accuracy and consistency between physical documents and digital records. Results showed that automated verification helps minimize errors and maintains data integrity as documents move across different departments. This study supports the development of SmartFlow by emphasizing the need for reliable verification features to ensure the accuracy of SmartFlow’s movement logs, mobile monitoring views, and audit trail aligned with each scan event.

**Libadia, M., et al. (2025).** Development of a web-based records management system: An ERMS initiative for the Philippines.

Libadia et al. (2025) studied the implementation of a web-based records management system for Philippine government institutions. Their findings revealed that web-based systems are highly effective for local government units because they enable secure and centralized access to records across multiple departments. This eliminates traditional communication barriers and allows real-time information sharing. This supports SmartFlow’s use of a centralized PHP/MySQL backend with Android mobile clients for daily operations and a planned web-based administrative dashboard for the Municipal Accountant (system administrator), connecting the Accounting, Budget, Human Resources, and Engineering offices  of the Municipality of Urbiztondo. 

**Piloton, A. J. L., et al. (2023).** Development of records tracking management system with QR code. (Implemented Records System).   
Piloton et al. (2023) studied how QR code technology can speed up data retrieval and improve organization in provincial government offices. They found that using scanning tokens is an efficient way to manage records, as it drastically cuts down on the time spent searching for files and prevents the disorganization common with manual logs. The researchers concluded that replacing legacy systems with automated tracking improves daily productivity. This research supports our project by providing an evidence-based argument for replacing manual logbooks in the Municipality of Urbiztondo with a faster, more efficient digital setup. 

**Rimando, M. K. V., & Corpuz, R. R. (2022).** A real time tracking system for school forms using QR codes with a watermarking algorithm. (Technical Thesis).   
Rimando and Corpuz (2022) designed a real-time tracking system that uses QR codes and watermarking to improve document security during transit. Their technical approach proved that adding mathematical validation and encryption to mobile tags prevents unauthorized changes or document forgery, making the routing process much more secure. They concluded that tracking systems must include these security measures to maintain data integrity. This study is a critical benchmark for SmartFlow, as it supports our goal of keeping sensitive municipal records—such as vouchers and payroll files—safe and authentic as they move through the LGU. 

**Castro, F. V,  Quilon, E. R. C., Arruejo, A. C.. et al. (2022) DocTrack: A dynamic document tracking system for the University of Northern Philippines.** (Implemented Tracking Project). 

Similar research created "DocTrack" a web-based system aimed to standardize their transactions **(Druke, Peralta and Alcid 2022\)**. At the core of their platform are functionalities around lifecycle, status and secure digital archiving. This work is very relevant to the SmartFlow project because its main architecture resembles our proposed LGU of Urbiztondo. This, in particular, validated our framework for integrating the modules to monitor document status. Furthermore, the fact that they comply with international standards is a good enough academic justification for us to use the ISO/IEC 25010 standard (now still used) as a basis of evaluating SmartFlow in terms of its security and performance efficiency.

**Pascual, J. M., et al. (2023).** NU DROP: A secure web-based document request and online payment system with QR-based cryptographic verification. (Technical Conference Paper).   
Pascual et al. (2023) developed NU DROP, a secure web-based document request and online payment system with QR-based cryptographic verification. Role-based dashboards and audit logs improved operational transparency in their web platform. For SmartFlow, this study supports the importance of role-based access, secure audit trails, and separate administrative monitoring (web dashboard for administrators, mobile client for field operations) when handling sensitive local government records such as financial vouchers and payrolls. 

**Urmeneta, J. A., Agullo, J., & et al. (2025).** Digitized Document Tracking System Using QR Code Technology and Graphic Draw (GD) Integration.

2025 Eight International Conference on Vocational Education and Electrical Engineering (ICVEE). Urmeneta et al. (2025) developed a digitized document tracking system that integrates QR code technology with Graphic Draw (GD) features to create secure and verifiable historical records. The system was designed to modernize document management by providing real-time monitoring, improved security, and better workflow efficiency. Their findings revealed that shifting from manual processes to an automated QR-based tracking system produces an accurate audit trail, making every document movement transparent and easily verifiable. The researchers concluded that such digital logging significantly enhances institutional accountability and simplifies validation procedures. This study is highly relevant to the present research as it provides strong technical and functional support for implementing a QR-based tracking system like SmartFlow, particularly in ensuring compliance with Commission on Audit (COA) standards through transparent and accountable document management in the Municipality of Urbiztondo.

**Foreign Studies**

**Hernandez, C., et al. (2023).** Implementing QR codes to improve sample tracking and data accessibility. (Implemented Technical Project).   
Hernandez et al. (2023) implemented QR codes with a centralized monitoring dashboard to improve sample tracking and data accessibility across sites. Their web-based dashboard applied to their laboratory workflow. For SmartFlow, the same principle applies in a different split: decentralized scanning on Android phones at each handoff, with centralized data in PHP/MySQL. Department heads and frontline staff use the mobile application for office-level monitoring; the Municipal Accountant and LGU system administrator are designed to use a web-based administrative dashboard for municipal-wide visibility (planned module; mobile monitoring). This supports administrative clarity and coordination among LGU departments without claiming that all users monitor through a single web page today. 

**Peltokorpi, J., et al. (2021).** QR code-based material flow monitoring in a subcontractor manufacturer network. (Technical Implementation Study).   
A study presented in 2021 shows that QR-based tracking frameworks exhibit industrial maturity and scaling-up potential for complex organisational networks. Their work further confirms that these architectures can reliably withstand large transaction loads without sacrificing data integrity or system performance. This research also serves as an important technical rationalization for what our mobile QR scanning framework will accomplish in the SmartFlow project. It guarantees the development team that our system is structurally sound and can be built upon. With this battle-tested architecture, we can scale in good faith multiple departments throughout the municipality with a reliable and efficient document tracking system across the local government unit.

**Synthesis of Related Studies**

Overall, the literature suggests that QR code technology is a practical way to manage documents in a government setting. In the Philippines, researchers like **Acedo (2025)** and **Piloton (2023)** show that QR-assisted tracking improves retrieval and workflow speed. International studies such as **Wibowo (2020)** and **Zare (2023)** emphasize reliable monitoring interfaces and evaluation through **ISO/IEC 25010**. For SmartFlow, these findings support **QR tagging, scan-based audit trails, mobile dashboards** for daily office work, and a **web-based administrative dashboard** for authorized administrators evaluated after the pilot using ISO/IEC 25010 principles and stakeholder feedback.

### **1.6.1 Conceptual Framework**

![][image1]  
***Figure 1.0:  IPO Conceptual Framework***

SmartFlow addresses manual inter-department routing of financial documents in the Municipality of Urbiztondo. The input consists of the knowledge, system, and hardware requirements needed to develop the hybrid application. The process covers document registration, QR-based tracking, audit trail recording, monitoring with alerts, and generation of COA-oriented reports. The output is the deployed SmartFlow system and improved document visibility and accountability.

**1.7 Technical Background**  
SmartFlow is a hybrid system that uses two client applications and one shared server. The Flutter mobile application is used at the point of document handoff, where a camera scans the QR code on the paper packet. The React web application is used for administration, monitoring, and reporting. Both applications connect to the same PHP and MySQL database so that every scan on mobile appears on the web dashboard in real time.

**System Architecture**

SmartFlow follows a three-tier architecture. The presentation layer includes the Flutter mobile app (Android smartphones) and the React web portal (desktop or laptop browsers). The application layer is the PHP REST API hosted on an Apache server at the LGU. The data layer is the MySQL database that stores users, offices, documents, scan logs, alerts, and report data. This design keeps scanning simple for frontline staff while giving the Municipal Accountant full control on the web.

**Flutter Mobile Application**

The Flutter framework uses the Dart programming language to build the mobile client installed on Android smartphones. Clerks and frontline staff in Engineering, HR, Budget, and Accounting use the app to log, receive and forward actions by scanning a QR code in seconds. Department heads and Accounting staff may also use the mobile app when they handle physical documents. The app sends scan data to the PHP API over the Wi-Fi. Flutter is chosen because it supports fast development, reliable camera-based QR scanning, and deployment on existing Android devices in the municipality.

**React Web Administrator Portal**

The React web application runs in a standard browser and serves as the main tool for the system administrator, Municipal Accountant, and department heads. Through the web portal, authorized users register financial documents, generate and print QR labels, view the real-time dashboard, configure processing time thresholds, receive delay alerts, and export COA-aligned flow summary reports and department analytics. React is used to build a responsive interface for dashboards and reports that are easier to manage on a larger screen than on a phone.

**PHP, MySQL, and Apache Server**

PHP handles server-side logic through a REST API that receives requests from Flutter and React. MySQL stores all system records, including document details, scan history, user accounts, office roles, and generated report figures. Apache serves the API and web files on a computer or local server provided by the LGU. When a QR code is scanned, the API writes an audit trail entry with the tracking identifier, office, personnel, timestamp, status, and remarks. The server then computes how long a document stayed in each office and whether it is overdue based on thresholds set on the web portal.

**QR Code Technology**

A QR (Quick Response) code is a two-dimensional barcode printed on the physical document folder and linked to one document record in SmartFlow. QR codes are generated when a document is registered. Rather than encoding a plain document identifier, SmartFlow encodes a cryptographically signed token in the format `SF1.{payload}.{hmac}`, where the payload carries the document identity, issuance time, and expiration date, and the HMAC signature is verified by the server on every scan. Tokens have a fixed validity period; expired tokens are rejected with a clear API error message, and reregistering or reprinting a document issues a fresh token. Scanning is inexpensive, fast, and does not require staff to type long reference numbers, which supports users with low technology knowledge as reported in the stakeholder interview.

**Reports, Audit Trail, and COA Support**

Each scan builds a chronological audit trail of document movement. The web portal aggregates this data to produce monthly, quarterly, and annual document flow summaries for COA support, including total documents processed, average processing time per department, late submission counts, and completion rates. These reports do not replace the financial statements prepared by the Accounting office.

**Security and Hosting**

SmartFlow uses authenticated login and role-based access control on both mobile and web. Connections use HTTPS in production; the server redirects HTTP to HTTPS on non-localhost environments and adds HSTS and security headers. QR tokens are signed using HMAC-SHA256 and verified server-side on every scan, so forged or tampered labels are rejected before any database write occurs. Tokens carry an expiration date and are refused after the validity period ends. The system enforces state-based scan rules — only valid document-state transitions are accepted — and a debounce guard blocks rapid duplicate scans. All scan events, whether accepted or rejected, are written to an audit log with reason codes. An administrative QR scan monitor dashboard allows the Municipal Accountant to review scan history, accepted and rejected events, and suspicious patterns, and to export records for compliance review. Printed QR labels display only the signed token, not personal data, in compliance with the Data Privacy Act of 2012. The LGU provides Android phones, printers, network access, and server hosting; hardware and hosting maintenance are outside the development scope of this study but are required for pilot operation.

**1.8 Definition of Terms**   
The following terms are used in this study.

* **Audit trail** — List of all scans for a document: office, user, date, time, and receive or forward action.  
* **Bottleneck department** — Office where documents stay too long or arrive late most often, based on web analytics.  
* **COA (Commission on Audit)** — National agency that audits LGU finances; SmartFlow gives flow reports only, not financial statements.  
* **Department performance analytics** — Web view of processing time, late counts, and delays per office.  
* **Document flow summary** — Monthly, quarterly, or annual COA support report from the web (volume, time per office, lates, completion rate).  
* **Financial documents** — Disbursement vouchers, payroll records, and approved budgets tracked in the pilot.  
* **Flutter mobile application** — Android app (Flutter/Dart) used to scan QR codes at document handoffs.  
* **Hybrid system** — Flutter mobile app plus React web portal sharing one PHP and MySQL server.  
* **Inter-department flow** — Movement of paper documents among Engineering, HR, Budget, and Accounting.  
* **ISO/IEC 25010** — Software quality standard used to evaluate SmartFlow in pilot testing.  
* **LGU (Local Government Unit)** — Local municipality; this study is conducted at the Municipality of Urbiztondo.  
* **Municipal Accountant** — Head of Accounting who collects documents from offices and prepares COA reports and also serves as the system administrator of SmartFlow (manages users, offices, roles, and processing-time thresholds).  
* **Overdue document** — Document that stayed in an office longer than the allowed days set on the web.  
* **PHP** — Server program in PHP that saves scan data and sends updates to mobile and web.  
* **Pilot offices** — Accounting, Budget, HR, and Engineering.  
* **Processing time threshold** — Maximum days a document may stay in one office before the system flags delay.  
* **QR code (Quick Response code)** — Printed code on the document folder linked to one system record.  
* **React web application** — Browser app to register documents, print QR, view dashboard, alerts, and reports.  
* **Scan-and-forward** — Scanning QR on the Flutter app when a document is received (scan-in) or forwarded (scan-out).  
* **SmartFlow** — QR-based hybrid system for tracking financial documents and supporting COA flow reporting in Urbiztondo.  
* **QR scan monitor** — Administrative dashboard showing all scan events (accepted and rejected) with who scanned, where, when, and the reason code for any rejection; used by the Municipal Accountant for compliance review and export.  
* **Signed QR token** — Cryptographically signed payload (`SF1.{payload}.{hmac}`) embedded in the printed QR label; contains document identity, issuance time, and expiration date, and is verified by the server on every scan to reject tampered or forged labels.  
* **State-based scan rules** — Logic that determines which scan action (IN or OUT) is valid based on the current document state; prevents illogical transitions such as scanning IN a document that is already IN.  
* **Duplicate scan prevention** — A state matrix combined with a debounce guard that blocks repeated scans of the same document in the same state within a short time window.  
* **Tracking identifier** — Unique document ID on the QR label (not personal data).

# **CHAPTER II**

# **METHODOLOGY**

**2.1 Design of Software, System, Product or Process**  
This section presents the design of SmartFlow as a hybrid document flow tracking system for the Municipality of Urbiztondo. The design covers software architecture, data flow diagrams, software development life cycle, system flowcharts, entity relationship diagram, and use case diagram. SmartFlow tracks physical financial documents disbursement vouchers, payroll records, and approved budgets among Engineering, Human Resources, Budget, and Accounting using QR codes 

**2.1.1 Software Architecture**

***Figure 2.1: SmartFlow Software Architecture***

SmartFlow uses a three-tier client–server architecture with two presentation clients and one shared backend. The presentation layer consists of a Flutter mobile application on Android smartphones for QR scan-in and scan-out at each office handoff, and a React web portal on desktop or laptop browsers for document registration, QR printing, real-time dashboard, delay alerts, COA-aligned flow reports, and department analytics. The application layer is a PHP REST API hosted on an Apache server at the LGU. It handles authentication, role-based access, document metadata, scan logging, threshold comparison, alert generation, and report aggregation. Both Flutter and React send and receive JSON over HTTPS on the municipal LAN or Wi-Fi. The data layer is a MySQL relational database storing users, roles, offices, documents, scan logs, processing thresholds, and alerts. This architecture supports the seven specific objectives in Chapter I: mobile scanning, web registration and QR tagging, dashboard and alerts, reports and analytics, and pilot evaluation. 

**2.1.2 Data Flow Diagram (DFD)**  
The Data Flow Diagram (DFD) shows how data move among users, SmartFlow processes, and data stores. At Level 0, the context diagram presents one process: the SmartFlow Document Tracking System and external entities that exchange data with it. At Level 1, the system is decomposed into subprocesses and eight data stores that correspond to the MySQL database. 

**![][image2]**

***Figure 2.2: SmartFlow DFD Level 0 (Context Diagram)***

Figure 2-2 presents the Level 0 Data Flow Diagram of SmartFlow. Process 0 represents the SmartFlow Document Tracking System. Four separate external entities represent frontline clerks in Engineering, Human Resources, Budget, and Accounting; each sends login credentials and scanned document records and receives authentication responses and scan confirmations through the Flutter mobile application. The Department Head requests document tracking and supervisory reports and receives department dashboard data and delay notifications. The Municipal Accountant, who also serves as the system administrator in the Urbiztondo pilot, sends document registration data, document status queries, COA report requests, user account settings, and system configuration data, and receives QR tracking codes, document flow status reports, COA compliance reports, export files, audit logs, and system status reports. The Commission on Audit receives COA support files from the Municipal Accountant outside the system. Internal data stores are shown in Figure 2-3.

**![][image3]**

**Figure 2.3: SmartFlow DFD Level 1**

Figure 2-3 presents the Level 1 Data Flow Diagram of SmartFlow, decomposing process 0 into five subprocesses and eight data stores. Process 1.0 registers documents and generates QR codes for the Municipal Accountant using D2 Offices, D4 Document Types, and D5 Documents. Process 2.0 records receive and forward scans from frontline clerks in E1 through E4, validates users through D3, appends D6 Scan Logs, and updates D5. Process 3.0 monitors document status using D5, D6, and D7 Thresholds, writes D8 Alerts, and sends dashboards and delay notifications to the Municipal Accountant and Department Head. Process 4.0 aggregates D5 and D6 to produce COA compliance reports, flow status reports, exports, and office analytics; the Accountant forwards COA support files to E8 outside the system. Process 5.0 maintains D1 Roles, D2 Offices, D3 Users, and D7 Thresholds for the Municipal Accountant in her role as system administrator.

# **2.1.3 Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC)**

**Figure 2.4. SmartFlow Agile SDLC Diagram**

The proponents applied a modified Agile (iterative) software development life cycle. Given a four-member development team and limited but recurring availability of the Municipal Accountant as client, a strict waterfall model would have delayed response to requirement clarifications, whereas a full Scrum implementation would have added process overhead disproportionate to the project scale. Iterative development with demonstrable releases after each cycle was therefore adopted.

The department member logs in to the Flutter mobile application. When a physical document arrives at the office, the clerk scans the QR code and selects the receipt. When the document is sent to another office, the clerk scans and selects forward. The system saves the audit trail and updates the dashboard. This flow is the same for any frontline staff who handle documents, regardless of office. Clerks do not register new documents or print QR labels in the primary workflow.

### **2.1.5 Entity Relationship Diagram (ERD)**

![][image7]  
***Figure 2.9 \-  SmartFlow Entity Relationship Diagram***

The Entity Relationship Diagram (ERD) defines the MySQL database for SmartFlow. The database has eight entities: roles, offices, users, document\_types, documents, scan\_logs, thresholds, and alerts.

Access and organization: users link to roles (municipal accountant/administrator, department head, clerk) and offices (Engineering, Human Resources, Budget, Accounting). In this pilot, the administrator and Municipal Accountant roles are assigned to the same user account.

Documents: documents link to document\_types (disbursement voucher, payroll record, approved budget) and to offices through origin\_office\_id and current\_office\_id. Each row has a unique tracking\_code for the QR label; surrogate primary key document\_id is used internally.

Tracking and compliance: scan\_logs design and record each receive or forward scan with office, user, and timestamp. thresholds store maximum processing hours per office and document type (set by the Municipal Accountant in her system administrator role) alerts store overdue notifications.

Document file content, financial statements, and predefined route tables are not stored in version 1\. COA flow reports and analytics are generated from documents and scan\_logs at report time.

**Figure 2.3.0 \-  Use Case Diagram**

**Primary use cases**

* Authenticate (sign in / sign out)  
* Register document and obtain document identifier  
* Scan QR code or enter document ID manually  
* Mark document IN or OUT  
* View document movement history  
* View per-office dashboard statistics  
* View overdue and follow-up alerts

Role-based access in the pilot build. User accounts include a role attribute (admin, staff, head). Role-restricted navigation is implemented in the prototype: staff accounts perform QR scanning and document forwarding; head accounts have access to office-level monitoring and queue views; admin accounts access the full municipal dashboard, COA reports, QR scan monitor, and system configuration. Operational assignment of registration and monitoring duties follows office policy during the pilot. 

**2.2 Requirements Analysis**

This section describes how requirements for SmartFlow were identified and how the current manual process differs from the proposed system. Requirements were gathered from the approved title proposal, related literature and studies cited in Chapter I, direct observation of document handling at the LGU, and qualitative data collection with stakeholders who route financial documents among pilot offices.

**Sources of Requirements**

### The researchers reviewed the seven specific objectives and scope limitations in the approved proposal. A semi-structured interview with the Municipal Accountant established the as-is workflow, pain points in locating documents, and expectations for Commission on Audit (COA) support. Follow-up interviews and observation with department heads and frontline clerks in Engineering, Human Resources, Budget, and Accounting are planned to confirm handoff points, typical processing duration per office, and acceptable threshold values for overdue alerts. Document analysis of sample disbursement vouchers, payroll records, and approved budgets uses metadata only (reference number, type, offices touched) not scanned file content to align registration fields and report categories with actual LGU practice. 

**As-Is Situation**

The Municipality of Urbiztondo has no existing Management Information System (MIS) that can monitor and track physical financial documents across offices. Basically, the movement of documents like disbursement vouchers , payroll records, approved budgets, and the supporting financial papers is handled the old way, by employees from different departments, one by one.

At present, if the Accounting Office or the department heads need to figure out where a document is, or what stage it’s in, they just rely on telephone calls, personal follow ups, and informal group chats. There is no real centralized log that records when documents are forwarded and when they’re received, so it becomes hard to watch the actual movement and processing progress in real time.

The Municipal Accountant usually ends up dealing with delays when documents don’t come in on time, mainly because there isn’t any automated, or shared, tracing mechanism that clearly captures when and where the documents were passed. Also, when routing histories and supporting records have to be prepared for Commission on Audit (COA) compliance, this is done mostly through manually updated Excel sheets, plus whatever employees can still remember. Because of that, the information may end up incomplete or even a bit off.

Furthermore, there’s no centralized database that can show real-time details about document location, processing duration, the responsible office , or the routing history itself. Without that, it’s not easy to spot bottlenecks, track document turnaround time, or compare departmental performance; everything tends to become subjective and time consuming. Overall, the present manual approach limits operational efficiency, transparency, and accountability in how financial documents are handled.

**To-Be Situation (SmartFlow)**

The proposed SmartFlow system, the Municipality of Urbiztondo will work on a centralized web and mobile document tracking solution, for checking the movement of physical financial papers among departments. Each included financial documents, like disbursement vouchers, payroll records, approved budgets, and the supporting documents, will be logged in the system first, and given a distinct tracking code which is then embedded in a print-able QR label when the document is created or handed in.

Document registration will typically be performed by the Municipal Accountant or an authorized encoder through the SmartFlow web portal. Once registered, every physical handoff between offices, including Engineering, Human Resources, Budget, and Accounting, will be recorded through QR code scanning using Android mobile devices. Clerks or authorized personnel will scan the QR code and select the appropriate action, such as receive or forward, to update the document’s status and location in real time.

Every scan event will be sent via a PHP-based API and then placed into the MySQL database, specifically under the scan\_logs table, so a full and practically unchangeable audit trail of the document trail and processing history is created. The React-based portal will also show an on-going active-document board, where you can see which office is handling the document right now, the time already spent, the routing history, and whether it is overdue based on turnaround limits set by the Municipal Accountant (system administrator).

The system will also generate automated delay alerts, and notifications for the Municipal Accountant plus the concerned department heads, whenever the documents go past the expected processing times. On top of that SmartFlow will produce COA aligned routing summaries, document history reports, and departmental performance analytics that can be exported into PDF or Excel formats, for audit help and reporting purposes.

Even if SmartFlow helps improve transparency, accountability, and efficiency in document monitoring, the physical documents themselves will still be the official legal records of the municipality. Version 1 of the system will just focus on document tracking and workflow monitoring, and it will not keep the document file contents, scanned images, or financial statement attachments inside the platform.

### **2.3 Requirements Documentation**

Requirements for SmartFlow are formally documented in the Software Requirements Specification (SRS), which expands the approved proposal into detailed functional and non-functional requirements, user roles, document types in scope, and pilot acceptance criteria. This section presents the summary required in Chapter II; the SRS serves as the reference during design, implementation, and user acceptance testing. 

**Document Types and User Roles (Scope)**

Version 1 tracks three document types: disbursement vouchers (typically originating from Engineering and routed toward Accounting), payroll records (typically from Human Resources toward Accounting), and approved budgets (typically from Budget toward Accounting). Exact office-to-office sequences may be refined after LGU confirmation; SmartFlow records actual scans rather than enforcing a fixed route table in the database.

User roles supported in the pilot are municipal accountant / system administrator (one user who registers documents, monitors flow, generates COA reports, and configures users, offices, and thresholds), department head (one office view), and frontline clerk (mobile scanning). An optional read-only auditor view may be enabled for export history without changing daily workflows.

**Functional Requirements**

| ID | Specific objective | Requirement statement |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| **FR-1** | Objective 1  QR tagging | The web portal shall register a financial document (document type, reference number, origin office, registration date) and generate a unique printable QR code tied to a tracking code. |
| **FR-2** | Objective 2  Scan-and-forward | The Flutter mobile application shall log each handoff with document identity, office, scanning user, timestamp, and action (receive or forward), appending an immutable audit trail. |
| **FR-3** | Objective 3  Dashboard | The web portal shall display all active documents with current location, elapsed time at the current office, and overdue status. |
| **FR-4** | Objective 4  Alerts | The web portal shall flag documents that exceed maximum processing hours per office and document type as set by the Municipal Accountant in her system administrator role. |
| **FR-5** | Objective 5  COA reports | The web portal shall produce monthly, quarterly, and annual flow summaries including totals processed, average time per department, late counts, and completion rates, without generating financial statements. |
| **FR-6** | Objective 6  Analytics | The web portal shall present department performance metrics such as submission speed, late counts, and bottleneck ranking. |
| **FR-7** | Objective 7  Evaluation | The system shall support user acceptance testing and data collection for ISO/IEC 25010–based evaluation among pilot participants. |

***Table 3.3 maps each functional requirement to the corresponding specific objective in Chapter I.***

Additional functional details in the SRS include search and filter by tracking code, document type, office, status, and date range; simple user interface for low technology familiarity; and export of reports to PDF or Excel for Accounting and COA support.

**Non-Functional Requirements**

| ID | Requirement |
| ----- | ----- |
| **NFR-01** | The Flutter application shall run on LGU-provided Android smartphones; the web portal shall run on desktop or laptop browsers (e.g., Chrome, Edge, Firefox). |
| **NFR-02** | QR scanning shall complete in seconds; interfaces shall require minimal training for clerks and heads. |
| **NFR-03** | The system shall provide secure login, role-based access control, cryptographically signed QR tokens with server-side signature and expiry verification, state-based scan validation with duplicate prevention, and HTTPS in production on the municipal network. |
| **NFR-04** | Audit logs (scan\_logs) shall be retained per LGU policy; handoff records shall not be casually deleted. |
| **NFR-05** | Server hardware, hosting, maintenance, and long-term backups are the responsibility of the LGU, not the research team. |

***Table 3.4 \-  Non-Functional Requirements of SmartFlow***

**2.4 Development and Pre-Testing Procedures**

Development and pre-testing ensure that SmartFlow modules align with FR-1 through FR-7 before full pilot evaluation described in Section 2.6. Work follows the iterative software development life cycle in Section 2.1.3, with seven increments mapped to the seven specific objectives.

**Development Procedures**

Development proceeds in the order below. Each step produces a testable artifact before the next increment begins.

1. Environment setup. Install and configure Apache, PHP 8, and MySQL on the development server; initialize the Flutter SDK and React project; maintain version control for source code and database scripts.  
2. Database implementation. Create tables and relationships per the entity relationship diagram (roles, offices, users, document\_types, documents, scan\_logs, thresholds, alerts); load seed data for pilot offices, document types, and default roles.  
3. API development. Implement PHP REST endpoints for authentication, user and office management, document registration and QR generation, scan submission, threshold and alert logic, dashboard queries, and COA-oriented report aggregation.  
4. Web development. Build React modules for document registration and QR printing (FR-1), municipal and office dashboards (FR-3), overdue alerts (FR-4), COA flow reports and exports (FR-5), department analytics (FR-6), and Municipal Accountant / administrator configuration (users, offices, thresholds).  
5. Mobile development. Build Flutter modules for clerk login, QR camera scan, receive and forward actions, and scan confirmation display (FR-2).  
6. Integration. Connect Flutter and React clients to the API over HTTPS on the municipal LAN or Wi-Fi; verify end-to-end flows from registration through multiple office scans to dashboard and report output.  
7. Revision. Correct defects identified in unit, integration, system, alpha, and user acceptance testing before deployment described in Section 2.5.

| Increment | Objective | Primary deliverable |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| **1** | QR tagging | Web registration and printable QR |
| **2** | Scan-and-forward | Flutter receive/forward with audit trail |
| **3** | Dashboard | Web active-document view |
| **4** | Alerts | Threshold rules and overdue notifications |
| **5** | COA reports | Monthly, quarterly, annual flow summaries |
| **6** | Analytics | Department performance and bottleneck views |
| **7** | Evaluation | UAT scripts and ISO/IEC 25010 questionnaire support |

***Table 3.5 \-  Development Increments for SmartFlow***

**Pre-Testing Procedures**

Pre-testing validates correctness, integration, and usability before the live pilot. 

| Test type | Procedure |
| ----- | ----- |
| Unit testing | Test individual API endpoints, QR and tracking code parsing, threshold comparison, alert creation, and report calculation functions with expected and edge-case inputs. |
| Integration testing | Execute Flutter scan → PHP API → MySQL → React dashboard and alert display on the LGU network; confirm role-based access restricts office heads to their office and clerks to scanning functions. |
| System testing | Run scripted test cases for FR-1 through FR-6 using sample disbursement vouchers, payroll records, and approved budgets; include incomplete scan scenarios to verify audit trail gaps are visible. |
| Alpha testing | Research team and capstone adviser validate each increment on a staging server; record defects and retest after fixes. |
| User acceptance testing (UAT) | Municipal Accountant, Accounting staff, department heads, and frontline clerks perform realistic tasks (register, print QR, receive scan, forward scan, view dashboard, generate export) using a structured UAT script. |
| Usability check | Time clerks completing register-and-scan and heads completing dashboard review; note errors and training needs for deployment training. |

***Table 3.6 \-  Pre-Testing Procedures for SmartFlow***

Pre-testing is considered complete when critical and high-severity defects are resolved, FR-1 through FR-7 are demonstrable, and UAT sign-off is obtained from the Municipal Accountant or designated LGU representative per the memorandum of agreement.

## **2.5 Implementation Plan (Infrastructure / Deployment)**

Implementation deploys SmartFlow on LGU infrastructure under a memorandum of agreement between the researchers and the Municipality of Urbiztondo. Hardware, network access, and ongoing server maintenance remain LGU responsibilities, as stated in Chapter I limitations.

**Infrastructure (LGU-Provided)**

| Component | Specification |
| ----- | ----- |
| **Application server** | PC or server running Apache, PHP 8, and MySQL for API and web hosting |
| **Network** | Municipal LAN or Wi-Fi reachable by pilot Android phones and office desktops |
| **Mobile devices** | Android smartphones with rear camera for QR scanning (at least one per scanning office) |
| **Web clients** | Desktop or laptop with modern browser for Accountant, heads, and administrator |
| **Printer** | Office printer for QR labels attached to physical document folders |
| **Security** | HTTPS certificate and firewall rules per LGU information technology policy |

***Table 3\. 7 \-  specifies infrastructure components required for the pilot.***

SmartFlow is designed for on-premise hosting at the LGU rather than public cloud dependency, so document metadata remains within municipal network control.

**Deployment Steps**

Deployment follows these steps in order:

1. Install and configure Apache, PHP, and MySQL on the LGU server with backup procedure documented for the Municipal Accountant (system administrator) and LGU IT.  
2. Deploy the database schema and seed pilot offices (Engineering, Human Resources, Budget, Accounting), roles, document types, and the initial Municipal Accountant / administrator account.  
3. Deploy the PHP REST API and production build of the React web application; enable HTTPS.  
4. Install the Flutter application (APK) on designated smartphones in each pilot office; verify camera permissions and network connectivity.  
5. Conduct hands-on training: Municipal Accountant / system administrator (users, thresholds, registration, dashboard, reports), department heads (office dashboard and alerts), and clerks (receive and forward scanning).  
6. Begin the pilot using live or controlled test documents per MOA schedule; document any skipped scans as a known limitation.  
7. Monitor server and application logs during the evaluation period; researchers provide support for configuration issues while LGU IT retains server access.

**Roles in Deployment**

The research team installs software, configures the initial database, prepares user guides, and delivers training sessions. LGU IT maintains server access and backups after handover. The Municipal Accountant, in her system administrator role, maintains user accounts and threshold updates inside SmartFlow, and also approves pilot timing, report formats, and participation of department representatives. Long-term hosting, hardware replacement, and electricity or connectivity costs are borne by the LGU after project completion.

#### 

## **2.6 Statistical Treatment of Data**

Evaluation of SmartFlow uses mixed methods. Qualitative data explain context and user perception; quantitative data from system logs and structured questionnaires measure process improvement and system quality. Subsections 2.6.1 through 2.6.5 follow the institutional outline for capstone methodology.

**2.6.1 Data Gathering Technique**

| Technique | Application |
| ----- | ----- |
| **Interview** | Semi-structured interview with the Municipal Accountant (conducted); follow-up with department heads and clerks on routing steps, volume, and acceptable processing times |
| **Observation** | Direct observation of physical document handoffs to confirm where receive and forward scans should occur |
| **Document analysis** | Review of sample disbursement vouchers, payroll records, and approved budgets using metadata fields only (no file digitization) |
| **System-generated data** | Extraction from MySQL during pilot: scan\_logs timestamps, dwell time between scans, alert counts, document completion status |
| **Questionnaire** | ISO/IEC 25010–based instrument with five-point Likert scale for usability and quality (Objective 7\) |

***Table 3.8 \-  Data Gathering Technique*** 

Qualitative findings support interpretation of as-is problems in Section 2.2. Quantitative log and questionnaire data support Objectives 5, 6, and 7 and COA-oriented reporting claims in later chapters.

**2.6.2 Setting of the Study**

The study is conducted at the Municipality of Urbiztondo, Pangasinan, Philippines. The operational setting comprises the Accounting Office, Budget Office, Human Resources Office, and Engineering Office—the four pilot departments that process disbursement vouchers, payroll records, and approved budgets that eventually support Municipal Accountant consolidation and Commission on Audit review. Data collection and system use occur during agreed pilot hours on LGU premises using municipal network resources.

**2.6.3 Subject of the Study**

Subjects are LGU personnel directly involved in financial document routing or system evaluation:

* Municipal Accountant and Accounting staff who register documents, monitor flow, and prepare COA support;  
* Department heads of Engineering, Human Resources, and Budget who supervise office performance;  
* Frontline clerks in Engineering, Human Resources, Budget, and Accounting who perform receive and forward scans;

Participation requires willingness to join under memorandum of agreement and informed consent. The study does not sample the general public; subjects are organizational actors in the document flow process.

**2.6.4 Sampling Technique**

The study employs purposive sampling, a non-probability technique in which participants are chosen because they hold roles essential to inter-department financial document flow in the four pilot offices. The Municipal Accountant serves as the key informant because Accounting is the convergence point for disbursement vouchers, payroll, and approved budgets before external audit support. Additional heads and clerks are included so each office contributes scanning behavior and supervisory feedback. A large random sample of residents is not required because the research question concerns organizational process and system acceptability, not citizen opinion.

**2.6.5 Statistical Treatment of Data**

Statistical treatment is descriptive and aligned with capstone reporting norms. Inferential hypothesis tests (e.g., t-test across municipalities) are not required unless the adviser approves a comparative design with a control LGU.

**A. Document Flow Metrics (System Logs)**

During the pilot, the researchers extract quantitative process variables from SmartFlow tables. Table 2.8 lists variables, sources, and statistical treatment.

| Variable | Source | Statistical treatment |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Total documents processed | documents | Frequency; percentage by document type (DV, payroll, budget) |
| Average processing time per office | scan\_logs (dwell between events) | Mean hours or days per office |
| Late submission count | Compare dwell time to thresholds | Frequency; percentage late per office |
| Completion rate | Completed vs. registered documents | Percentage |
| Bottleneck office | Highest mean delay or highest late percentage | Ranking |

These metrics support Specific Objectives 5 and 6 and provide evidence for COA-aligned flow summaries.

**B. Usability and Quality Evaluation (Questionnaire)**

Pilot participants complete a questionnaire mapped to ISO/IEC 25010 quality characteristics: functional suitability, performance efficiency, compatibility, usability, reliability, security, maintainability, and portability. Each item uses a five-point Likert scale (for example, 5 \= Strongly Agree, 1 \= Strongly Disagree).

Weighted mean (WM) summarizes responses per characteristic and overall, using WM \= Σ (w × x) / Σ w, where w is the weight assigned to an item and x is the numeric Likert value. Frequency and percentage describe the distribution of responses per item. Ranking orders offices or criteria by mean score or by delay metrics from system logs.

Interpretation of weighted means follows the verbal description scale approved by the research adviser (for example, 4.21–5.00 as Strongly Agree, 3.41–4.20 as Agree, 2.61–3.40 as Uncertain, 1.81–2.60 as Disagree, 1.00–1.80 as Strongly Disagree). The researchers shall confirm exact cutoffs with the adviser before final write-up.

**C. Effectiveness Comparison (Before vs. After Pilot)**

Where baseline information exists from the Municipal Accountant interview (such as estimated weekly follow-up calls or average time to locate a document), the study may report descriptive before-and-after comparison using percentage change during the pilot period. This comparison is illustrative rather than inferential unless a formal control group is defined.

**D. Tools for Computation**

Tabulation and computation may use Microsoft Excel, Google Sheets, or SPSS if required by the college research office. SmartFlow export to Excel allows the Municipal Accountant to verify selected report figures against manual records for the same period
